introduction: China Town is a projected photographic animation with sound, made from thousands of digital photographs. The photographs were taken by the artist Lucy Raven in quick succession and are animated in such a way that each stays on screen for a different duration but for no more than a few seconds. This gives the projection a peculiar rhythm rather than a regular or repetitive one. The jolty appearance of the photographs is emphasised by the contrast with the sound, which is continuous.The photographs track the process of the production of copper wire, from the mining of ore in Nevada, through the transportation of the ore from Vancouver, to China where it is smelted and refined. Raven’s work represents the conditions of labour in different countries and points to the anomalies of production in the early twenty-first century, a moment when China, a country in economic ascendancy, is still used by an economic superpower (North America) to process its raw materials.The artist’s primary motivation in addressing this subject was to question the rhetoric of the ‘wireless’ age and to examine the exhaustion of natural and human resources. It is one of the myths of the present time that we are less dependent on raw materials and human labour, since our media devices such as smartphones, IPads and laptops are now ‘wireless’. As we consume, create and distribute digital information with these devices, we are persuaded more and more to forget about the materials that run them, and on which their operations depend. Sceptical about this rhetoric Raven focused on the copper wires that enable ‘wireless’ communications, and on the people who labour to produce copper wire. Her research took her from her home country of America, across the Pacific. Her concerns in this work are close to those of Steve McQueen, whose film Gravesend 2007 (Museum of Modern Art, New York) looks at the mining of coltan – a mineral used in computers – in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Simon Starling, who has also made work on the subject of the mining and refining of metals such as aluminium.Raven’s work is also part of a tradition of American art concerned with documenting economic and manufacturing processes, recalling in particular the work of Allan Sekula. Like Sekula, Raven is interested in the line between documentary and fine art practice. A straight documentary film maker might be drawn to the subject examined in China Town, but Raven’s decision to animate her material reveals an interest in the medium of representation as much as the subject represented. The viewer is invited to question why the artist made China Town as an animation rather than as a continuous film. The animation is the result of the artist’s painstaking editorial activity, especially given the unequal duration of each photograph during the projection. It therefore reinforces through its production the ideas of materiality and labour which make up the subject of the film.https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/raven-china-town-t13799
